title: AI assistants check
instructions: Five questions on what assistants are, where they fail, and how to use them safely.

questions.prompt: What is a coding assistant fundamentally doing when it writes code?
options: Running your program to check it works
Producing the text most likely to follow your prompt, based on patterns it learned
Looking up the single correct answer in a database
Understanding your whole project automatically
questions.explanation: A language model predicts likely text. It does not run your code or know the one correct answer unless it is given tools to do so.

questions.prompt: An assistant answers in a very confident tone. What does that tell you about whether the answer is correct?
options: It is probably correct
Nothing, because the tone is the same whether it is right or wrong
It was verified by experts
It was checked by running it
questions.explanation: Fluent, confident writing is what the model produces either way. Only checking tells you whether it is correct.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the safest to paste into an AI chat?
options: Your database password
A function where the real API key has been replaced with YOUR_API_KEY
Your .env file
A list of customer email addresses
questions.explanation: Replace secrets and personal data with placeholders first. Anything real that you paste should be treated as shared.

questions.prompt: What does the context window limit?
options: How many files you can store on disk
How much text the assistant can take into account at once
How fast your internet connection is
How many people can use the assistant
questions.explanation: The assistant can only consider a limited amount of text at a time. Anything you did not include, or that fell out of a long conversation, is not seen.

questions.prompt: An assistant wrote a function and you commit it to your project. Who is responsible for it?
options: You
The assistant
The company that made the assistant
Nobody, it was generated
questions.explanation: The person who accepts and ships the code owns it. That is why you read, test and understand it first.

title: Redact secrets before pasting
instructions:
Write `redact(text)`. It returns the text with every word that **starts with `sk-`** replaced by `[REDACTED]`. Words are separated by single spaces, and everything else stays exactly as it was.

```text
redact('key is sk-abc123 ok')  ->  'key is [REDACTED] ok'
```

There is nothing to print. Your function is tested directly.

tests.description: leaves text without a key unchanged
